lines.text: Join two tables, both split into matching pieces, and there are two ways to do it.
Combine everything first, then join.
Or join each matching piece on its own, and skip the combining entirely.
Neither plan here is cutting corners. Both of them touch every row, apply the same condition, and land on the same answer.
So why would cutting that work into four smaller pieces ever come out ahead of handling it as one piece?
Each smaller join's own table of matching rows can fit somewhere the one big combined table can't.
The total amount of work doesn't change. How it gets divided up is what decides whether it fits in memory at all.
Turn the setting off, and the plan shows one join sitting above everything from both tables, stitched together first.
Turn it on, and that single join becomes four separate ones, each handling just its own matching slice.
This only works when the condition joining the two tables covers every piece they're split on, and both tables are split the exact same way.
Once that's true, a row on one side can only ever match a row that's already sitting in the exact same piece on the other.
There's nothing left to check across the different pieces — each one is already a complete, self-contained problem.
Give both versions of the plan the exact same, fairly tight amount of memory to work with.
The one combined table of matching rows doesn't fit, and has to spill out to disk.
Each of the four smaller ones does fit, with room to spare. Same hardware, same memory limit, same answer in the end.
Take that same idea up a level: two tables, each sitting across several different machines instead of pieces on one.
If those tables aren't already split up the same way across those machines, what has to happen before they can even be joined?
Data has to physically move across the network first.
A single machine's matching pieces give you that alignment for free. Across separate machines, something has to go build it.
A system built to run across many machines writes this step right into its own plan, with a name.
One kind of step redistributes data by running it through a hash function, so matching rows end up together.
A different kind just copies one whole side out to every machine involved. The plan itself tells you exactly which one is happening, and where.
Redistributing by hash means taking both sides of the join and spreading each one out across every machine, sorted by the join key.
Once that's done, every machine is holding exactly the rows that could possibly match each other, locally.
That's the network doing, by force, the exact same thing a single machine's matching pieces already had for nothing.
There's a cheaper option, though, when one side of the join is small.
Instead of redistributing both sides, just copy the small one, whole, out to every machine.
Nothing about the bigger side has to move anywhere at all.
A query has been copying one side of a join out to every machine, because it's small.
That side keeps growing, past the point the system considers small.
What should happen next?
Switch over to redistributing both sides instead.
Past a certain size, copying something out to every machine costs more than just moving everything once, properly aligned.
One widely used system draws that line at ten megabytes by default — below it, copy; above it, redistribute.
That's not a vague guideline. It's a real number, and it can be changed, or turned off entirely.
Some systems can even cross that line mid-query, switching strategy the moment they see a side's actual size, rather than only guessing beforehand.
Step back and this is the exact same story as the one at the very start, just at a different scale.
Tables already split the same way need nothing extra done to them before a join, whether that split is across pieces on one machine, or across separate machines entirely.
It's the same alignment, paying off the same way, however far apart the pieces actually sit.
Matching pieces mean less duplicated work on a single machine.
Spread across separate machines, a join needs something to move data first, unless that alignment is already there.
One way to do that redistributes everything. The other just copies the small side.
And which one happens isn't locked in ahead of time — it can genuinely change once the real sizes are known.
A plan names one of its steps by the kind of redistribution it's doing, and the name reads as a hash-based spread, not a copy.
Is this step copying one side of a join out to every machine, or spreading both sides out by the join key?
Spreading both sides out by the join key.
A hash-based spread redistributes; copying one side everywhere gets its own separate name in the plan, and this isn't it.
One side of a join comes in well under the size a system is willing to copy out to every machine.
Should that side get copied everywhere, or should both sides get redistributed instead?
Copied everywhere.
Sitting comfortably under that limit is exactly the case copying exists for — redistributing both sides would just be doing more work for no reason.
